beats.text: The most common way to understand probability, and the one most of us meet first, is to see it as a frequency.
beats.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency

beats.text: In this view, when you say the chance of heads is one half, you are saying that if you flipped this coin many, many times, the share of heads would settle closer and closer to one half.
beats.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency

beats.text: Flip it ten times, and you might well get seven heads.
beats.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency

beats.text: Flip it a hundred times, and the share is already closer.
beats.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency

beats.text: Flip it a million times, and it is practically glued to fifty percent.
beats.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency

beats.text: People have actually done this, by hand.
beats.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency

beats.text: In the eighteenth century, the naturalist Buffon flipped a coin four thousand and forty times, and got two thousand and forty-eight heads.
beats.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency

beats.text: The statistician Karl Pearson flipped twenty-four thousand times, and got twelve thousand and twelve.
beats.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency

beats.text: And during the Second World War, a mathematician named John Kerrich, held in an internment camp in Denmark, flipped ten thousand times, and got five thousand and sixty-seven heads.
beats.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency

beats.text: Every one of them, a hair away from one half.
beats.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency

beats.text: This is the law of large numbers, first proved by Jacob Bernoulli in a book published in seventeen thirteen.
beats.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency

beats.text: It says that the frequency you observe will converge to the theoretical value as the number of trials grows.
beats.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency

beats.text: This way of seeing things is enormously useful, and a huge number of systems around us are built on it.
beats.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
beats.section: The world that runs on frequencies

beats.text: A casino makes money not because it cares who wins this round, but because it cares about millions of rounds.
beats.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
beats.section: The world that runs on frequencies

beats.text: An insurance company doesn't need to know whether you will have an accident. It needs to know how many, out of a million customers, will.
beats.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
beats.section: The world that runs on frequencies

beats.text: A factory checking the quality of its products works by the very same logic.
beats.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
beats.section: The world that runs on frequencies

beats.text: The key thing in all these examples is that they can be repeated.
beats.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
beats.section: The world that runs on frequencies

beats.text: You can keep flipping the coin, keep making new batches, keep selling new insurance policies.
beats.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
beats.section: The world that runs on frequencies

beats.text: That repeatability turns a frequency into a number you can measure and test, so any argument can be settled with real data.
beats.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
beats.section: The world that runs on frequencies

beats.text: For problems of this kind, the frequency view is almost the natural choice. The trouble lies with the problems that are not of this kind.
beats.act: ACT ONE — Probability as frequency
beats.section: The world that runs on frequencies

beats.text: Try applying the frequency view to sentences like these.
beats.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath

beats.text: The probability that it rains in Hanoi tomorrow is seventy percent.
beats.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath

beats.text: The probability that a new drug passes its phase three trial is thirty percent.
beats.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath

beats.text: The probability that this candidate wins the election is sixty percent.
beats.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath

beats.text: There is only one tomorrow, and it will not repeat.
beats.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath

beats.text: That drug is tested only once, in exactly the way it is being tested.
beats.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath

beats.text: That election happens exactly once in history. There are no million tomorrows for you to count how many were rainy.
beats.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath

beats.text: People who hold the frequency view have a rather clever answer for the weather.
beats.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath

beats.text: They say the seventy percent is not about tomorrow at all. It is about the whole collection of days on which the forecast said seventy percent.
beats.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath

beats.text: If, among all those days, roughly seven in ten really did turn out rainy, the forecast is called well calibrated.
beats.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath

beats.text: It is a lovely idea, and it is exactly how forecasting models are scored in practice.
beats.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath

beats.text: But that answer cannot rescue every case.
beats.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath

beats.text: Go back to the coin lying under my hand. It has already landed. There is no collection to put it in.
beats.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
beats.section: Back to the coin under my hand

beats.text: The event has happened, and the result is fixed.
beats.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
beats.section: Back to the coin under my hand

beats.text: And this is the point where I feel I need to stop and think a little harder.
beats.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
beats.section: Back to the coin under my hand

beats.text: Suppose I sneak a look at the coin, and you don't.
beats.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
beats.section: Back to the coin under my hand

beats.text: For me, the probability is now one hundred percent, or zero. For you, it is still fifty.
beats.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
beats.section: Back to the coin under my hand

beats.text: The coin did not change at all in the instant I looked. Only the information changed.
beats.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
beats.section: Back to the coin under my hand

beats.text: And that small observation leads straight to the second way of understanding probability.
beats.act: ACT TWO — Where frequency runs out of breath
beats.section: Back to the coin under my hand

beats.text: The second view says that probability measures how strongly you believe a statement, given the information you have.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: A property of you, not of the coin

beats.text: In this view, probability is a property of the relationship between you and the event. It doesn't live inside the coin, or the cloud, or the ballot.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: A property of you, not of the coin

beats.text: It describes the state of your knowledge.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: A property of you, not of the coin

beats.text: At first this sounds far too loose, as if anyone could believe whatever they like.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief

beats.text: But in fact it is tightly constrained.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief

beats.text: In the nineteen twenties and thirties, Frank Ramsey in England and Bruno de Finetti in Italy, working independently, showed that if you want your beliefs to be consistent, they are forced to obey exactly the rules of probability.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief

beats.text: Their argument is built on betting.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief

beats.text: Suppose you are willing to bet according to exactly how strongly you believe things.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief

beats.text: Now suppose your numbers break the rules. In a match with only two possible outcomes, you believe team A will win with seventy percent, and at the same time you believe team B will win with fifty percent.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief

beats.text: Then someone can sell you two tickets. One pays a dollar if A wins, and by your own belief it is worth seventy cents. The other pays a dollar if B wins, and by your own belief it is worth fifty cents.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief

beats.text: Each ticket looks perfectly fair to you, so you buy both, for a dollar twenty.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief

beats.text: But exactly one team will win, so you will collect exactly one dollar. Whatever happens, you lose twenty cents.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief

beats.text: So the rules of probability don't fall from the sky. They are the conditions for your beliefs not to contradict themselves.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief

beats.text: What I love about this view is that it handles events that happen only once.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief

beats.text: You can perfectly well talk about how strongly you believe that Mars once had life, even though that is simply true or false, and will never be repeated.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief

beats.text: Once probability is a belief, a new question appears. When new information arrives, how much should you change your mind?
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: Bayes' theorem answers that question. Let me walk through a concrete situation, so it is easy to picture.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: A text message pops up on your phone, claiming to be from your bank.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: The hypothesis you are weighing is this. The message is a scam.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: Until now, messages from this number have almost always been genuine, so your starting belief leans heavily towards genuine.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: Picture it as a pair of scales, tipped deep to one side.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: The message opens with "Dear valued customer". So you ask yourself two questions.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: First, if this is a scam, how likely is it to open so politely? Quite likely.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: Second, if this is genuine, how likely is it to open exactly like that? Also quite likely.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: The ratio between those two answers is the weight of the evidence.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: Here the two numbers are almost equal, so the ratio is close to one. Multiply the scales by it, and they barely move.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: You have read the greeting, and you have really learned nothing.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: You read on, and the message asks you to reply with your one-time password.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: If it is a scam, that request makes perfect sense. If it is really your bank, it almost never happens.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: Now the two numbers are far apart, the weight is large, and the scales swing hard.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: That is the heart of Bayes' theorem.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: A piece of evidence is convincing not because it fits your hypothesis, but because it would be unlikely if your hypothesis were wrong.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: A sign that shows up about equally often whether the hypothesis is true or false tells you almost nothing, however impressive it looks.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: And one more thing. The scales only shift. They are never reset from scratch.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: If you start from a hypothesis that is extremely unlikely, with the scales tipped very deep, a single piece of evidence is usually not enough to pull them back to the middle.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: That sounds obvious. But in the next part I will show you just how easily it gets forgotten.
beats.act: ACT THREE — Probability as degree of belief
beats.section: Evidence doesn't tell you right or wrong, it shifts the scales

beats.text: Here is a classic example from medicine.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: Suppose there is a disease that affects one person in every thousand. And there is a test for it.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: If you really have the disease, the test comes back positive ninety-nine percent of the time.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: If you are perfectly healthy, there is still a five percent chance it comes back positive by mistake.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: You take the test, and it comes back positive. What do you think is the chance that you really have the disease?
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: The easiest way to see it is to count real people.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: Imagine one hundred thousand people all taking the test.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: About one hundred of them really have the disease, and the test catches ninety-nine of them.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: That leaves ninety-nine thousand nine hundred healthy people. With a five percent false alarm rate, about four thousand nine hundred and ninety-five of them get a positive result too.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: So in total, about five thousand and ninety-four people are holding a positive result. And only ninety-nine of them are actually sick.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: Ninety-nine out of five thousand and ninety-four, is about two percent.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: In other words, even with a positive result in your hand, the chance that you are really ill is only about two percent.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: That number surprises a lot of people, and not only beginners.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: In nineteen seventy-eight, researchers at Harvard put almost exactly this question to sixty doctors, residents and medical students. Nearly half of them answered ninety-five percent.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: The reason is that most of us focus on how accurate the test is, and forget how rare the disease was to begin with.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: That starting rate matters enormously, yet it slips out of view without a sound.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: When a disease is rare, the healthy people are so numerous that just a few percent of false alarms is enough to swamp the people who are truly sick.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: And notice what made it easy. Counting people, instead of juggling percentages.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: Psychologists call these natural frequencies, and simply rewriting the problem this way makes far more people get it right.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: Counting, the frequency view, turns out to be the best tool for updating a belief.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: The lesson of this example is that the same test result can mean very different things, depending on the background information you start from.
beats.act: ACT FOUR — The number that surprises experts

beats.text: By now you might think these two views are two rival schools of mathematics. In fact, they are not.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides

beats.text: In nineteen thirty-three, Andrey Kolmogorov put probability on a rigorous mathematical foundation, built on just three axioms, and they are surprisingly simple.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides

beats.text: He said that a probability is a rule that gives every event a number, such that, first, no value is ever negative.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides

beats.text: Second, the certain event gets the value one.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides

beats.text: And third, for events that are mutually exclusive, meaning they can't happen together, the probability that one of them happens is the sum of their separate probabilities.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides

beats.text: That is all.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides

beats.text: The whole of modern probability theory is built on those three conditions.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides

beats.text: And what is remarkable is that nowhere in those three axioms is there a single line saying what probability means.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides

beats.text: Kolmogorov gives you the rules of the game, not its meaning.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides

beats.text: Seen from mathematics, a probability is just a measure, from the same family as the way we measure area and volume, with the convention that the whole space of outcomes has measure one.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides

beats.text: When you say an event has probability three tenths, you are saying it takes up three tenths of that space.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides

beats.text: The frequency view and the belief view both satisfy these axioms.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides

beats.text: That is why the two sides can argue fiercely about meaning, and still share the very same set of tools for calculation.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides

beats.text: Frequentists and Bayesians build different statistical methods, and answer different questions. But neither of them is doing the mathematics wrong.
beats.act: ACT FIVE — Mathematics doesn't take sides

beats.text: There is a deeper question, and to me it is the most fascinating question in this whole video.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?

beats.text: A coin flying through the air is a physical object obeying Newton's mechanics.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?

beats.text: If you knew exactly the force of the flick, the angle, the spin, the height, and the way the hand catches it, you could calculate the result. There is nothing mysterious in it at all.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?

beats.text: Persi Diaconis, a mathematician who was once a professional magician, showed this in a very practical way.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?

beats.text: He and his colleagues built a coin-tossing machine with fixed settings, and it gave the same face every single time.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?

beats.text: His team also showed that a coin flipped by hand and caught in the palm is slightly biased towards the face that started on top, about fifty-one percent of the time.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?

beats.text: In twenty twenty-three, a team of researchers tested this with more than three hundred and fifty thousand real flips, and found fifty point eight percent. Almost exactly what the theory predicted.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?

beats.text: So if you had seen which face was up when I flicked my coin at the start of this video, your number would not be fifty percent. It would be fifty-one.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?

beats.text: The coin is the same coin. Once again, only the information changed.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?

beats.text: So the randomness of a coin is not inside the coin.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?

beats.text: It lies in the fact that the result is extremely sensitive to starting conditions that our hands cannot control, and our eyes cannot measure.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?

beats.text: Randomness, here, is another name for missing information.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?

beats.text: With the weather, with markets, with traffic, the story is much the same. They are complicated, and extremely sensitive to where they start, but they are not mystical.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?

beats.text: To be fair, there is one place where this story is not settled.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
beats.section: The one place the story isn't settled

beats.text: Down at the scale of single particles, quantum mechanics behaves very differently.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
beats.section: The one place the story isn't settled

beats.text: Experiments built on a result called Bell's theorem, which earned the Nobel Prize in Physics in twenty twenty-two, have ruled out the idea that each outcome is simply written in advance, in hidden information the particles carry with them.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
beats.section: The one place the story isn't settled

beats.text: Whether that is true randomness, or something stranger still, physicists are still debating.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
beats.section: The one place the story isn't settled

beats.text: But a coin is not an electron. For the coin, the weather and almost everything in our daily lives, the uncertainty lives in us.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
beats.section: The one place the story isn't settled

beats.text: So, in the end, probability is often introduced as a tool for talking about how random the world is.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
beats.section: The distance between you and the coin

beats.text: But look closely, and it is a disciplined way of writing down what you don't yet know.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
beats.section: The distance between you and the coin

beats.text: The fifty percent at the start of this video says nothing about the coin. It describes the distance between you, and the coin.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
beats.section: The distance between you and the coin

beats.text: Thank you for watching all the way to the end.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
beats.section: The distance between you and the coin

beats.text: If this changed the way you hear the word probability, subscribe to ninety-nine percent from scratch, so you don't miss the next one. See you soon.
beats.act: ACT SIX — Is the world random, or are we just missing information?
beats.section: The distance between you and the coin
